title: Mushroom-based high-efficiency solar evaporator for water harvesting
abstract: Solar-driven interfacial evaporation represents an innovative and highly promising strategy to address global freshwater scarcity and enhance water purification technologies. The distinctive structure of natural mushrooms, comprising a pileus and stipe, offers a feasible pathway for designing efficient and low-cost solar evaporators. In this work, natural mushrooms were employed as solar evaporators to evaluate their performance in evaporating seawater and sewage. Under 3.9 suns illumination, evaporation rates of 4.89, 4.57, and 3.73 kg·m −2 ·h −1 were achieved for sewage, deionized water, and seawater, respectively. Under natural sunlight conditions (0.5 sun), the mushroom evaporator attained rates of 2.62 and 2.13 kg·m −2 ·h −1 for sewage and seawater, respectively. The mushroom-based evaporator demonstrates not only exceptional photothermal conversion performance but also remarkable cycling stability and durability.

title: A comprehensive review of hydrogen integrated hybrid renewable energy systems: Configurations, models, simulation and optimization with artificial intelligence
abstract: This work presents a comprehensive review of hydrogen-based hybrid renewable energy systems (HRESs), covering mathematical models, simulation and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven optimization approaches. Emphasizing the potential of hydrogen as an energy carrier to deepen renewable energy integration, especially in solar and wind HRESs, this review systematically details mathematical models for various renewable generation and storage systems, serving as a structured reference for researchers. Given the complexity of HRES modeling, this work provides insights into different modeling software and optimization algorithms, with a particular focus on artificial intelligence methods. The integration of software and artificial intelligence promises to solve complex modeling and optimization challenges with potential applications in different environments. Future directions suggest that the physical model-assisted AI framework, which embeds physical principles within AI models, holds promise for enhancing prediction accuracy and reliability in HRES applications. This framework, especially when combined with stochastic optimization, offers a potential pathway to address challenges in data availability and computational complexity, supporting the effective design and optimization of hydrogen-based HRESs for real-world applications. The overall findings will help improve the design and optimization of hydrogen-based hybrid renewable energy systems for practical implementation.

title: OpenFOAM-based study on near-field formation and mixing of high nozzle pressure ratio hydrogen jets from leakages
abstract: A gas stored at high-pressure leaking through a small hole forms a complex series of shock structures as it accelerates and expands to ambient conditions. The near-field region of the jet includes the initial jet expansion, Mach disc formation, and starting vortices, all of which can affect hydrogen mixing with the surrounding air and have an associated combustion risk. Through the use of a modified OpenFOAM solver, simulations of hydrogen stored at 10 bar and 100 bar leaking into atmospheric conditions through 1.5 mm diameter circular nozzles were performed to determine the transient temperature profile, shock locations, and hydrogen mixing profiles of the hydrogen jet in its initial expansion and propagation stages. From these transient simulations, it was shown that starting vortices form pockets of mixed hydrogen and air that are within hydrogen flammability limits. This new simulation data shows mixed hydrogen pockets can linger in the nozzle near-field region and present a flammability risk that is not easily accounted for when using existing numerical models optimized for far-field flame behavior, showing this new open-source tool can resolve hydrogen mixing behavior in the nozzle near-field region without compromising on shock resolution capabilities. • Existing OpenFOAM solver modified to simulate high-pressure hydrogen leaks. • Transient numerical data for the highly-underexpanded hydrogen jets captured. • Mixing vortices are observed to shed pockets of mixed hydrogen and air. • Potentially flammable hydrogen pockets observed to linger near the nozzle.

title: Flamelet/progress variable modelling of turbulent non-premixed cool flames of dimethyl-ether/methane mixtures
abstract: In present work, the turbulent non-premixed cool flames of dimethyl-ether (DME)/methane mixtures are studied within the framework of flamelet/progress variable modelling and chemical kinetic analyses. The numerical setup is based on the Princeton CARAT burner configuration, and the accuracy of the hpmech-V3.3 chemistry to model turbulent low-temperature combustion is validated against the reference experiments and DNS. The simulation results reveal that turbulent cool flame structures are modified (lifted) by methane addition owing to the decline of cool flame extinction limits. The different flame regions associated with differing thermochemical characteristics for the dual-fuel lifted cool flames are uncovered. The DME/methane consumption trends suggest that methane addition inhibits the DME low-temperature oxidation. Through the kinetic analyses, the mechanisms are identified to be two-fold: methane competes with the DME H-abstraction reaction for OH radicals and the reaction of QOOH <=> O 2 + 2CH 2 O is significantly slowed down with the methane addition. The mechanisms also kinetically explain the finding that the formation of CH 2 O, CO, CO 2 in cool flames decline in response to the increase of methane blending ratios. The correlation between temperature and key intermediate formation is discovered. • Turbulent cool flame structures are modified (lifted) by methane addition through the decline of cool flame extinction limits. • The different flame regions associated with differing thermochemical characteristics for the dual-fuel lifted cool flames are uncovered. • Methane addition inhibits the DME low-temperature oxidation. • The kinetic mechanisms behind are identified: CH 4 competes with the DME H-abstraction reaction for OH radicals and the reaction of QOOH <=> O 2 + 2CH 2 O is significantly slowed down with the methane addition.

title: Corrigendum to “Effect of rich-MgO from low-calcium limestone on the calcination and properties of C4A3$-C2S clinker” [Green energy and Resources 2 (2024) 100099]
Biochar for heavy metal remediation in aquatic and terrestrial environments: Properties, influencing factors, and mechanisms
abstract: With the rapid development of industrialization, heavy metal pollution in water and soil has become increasingly serious. Biochar has attracted extensive attention for its application in heavy metal remediation, which mainly depends on its developed porous structure, large specific surface area, abundant functional groups and minerals. This review outlines the status of heavy metal pollution and summarize the key physicochemical characteristics of biochar. Subsequently, a detailed analysis was conducted on the critical influencing factors, encompassing biochar physicochemical properties, environmental parameters, and heavy metal attributes. The core section comprehensively examines the primary remediation mechanisms, such as physical adsorption, ion exchange, precipitation, and complexation, highlighting how their relative importance shifts with biochar type and environmental context. Furthermore, remediation performance is not governed by a single mechanism but by the synergistic interplay of biochar's evolving surface chemistry, solution conditions, and metal speciation. Additionally, differences in dominant mechanisms and long-term stability are critically compared between aquatic and soil systems. Finally, we identify current knowledge gaps—particularly concerning short-term field performance, long-term aging effects, and sustainability under real-world conditions—and propose targeted future research directions to advance the practical, scalable, and safe application of biochar in heavy metal remediation.

title: Towards green marine engines: A review of methanol fueled internal combustion engine
abstract: With the global marine industry actively exploring sustainability and making efforts to move towards decarbonization goals, identifying suitable alternative fuels has become a crucial task. Among the numerous types of clean fuels, methanol has become a transitional fuel for the maritime sector to achieve decarbonization goals due to its superior combustion properties. Additionally, methanol has a wide range of sources. It can be produced from coal, natural gas and biomass and its production capacity is distributed all over the world. Asia (with China as the main country), the Middle East and North America are the major bases. In recent years, the production capacity of renewable methanol has been gradually increasing. Renewable methanol is of great significance for achieving carbon neutrality. This review conducts a detailed collation of different types of methanol engines, comparatively analyzes their performance under various operating conditions, and draws corresponding conclusions. The key characteristic parameters encompass ignition delay, knocking, brake thermal efficiency, indicated thermal efficiency, in-cylinder pressure, heat release rate, nitrogen oxides, soot, and carbon monoxide. Based on the examined results, compared with diesel engines, methanol engines exhibit superior performance in terms of emissions. However, methanol fueled engine reduces the thermal efficiency in some cases, which needs more new technologies to improve the efficiency.

title: Residential energy consumption dynamics: A SHAP-based interpretation, k-means clustering, and predictive modelling
abstract: A proper understanding of climatic consumption dynamics is critical for demand-side management, grid stability, and climate-sensitive residential energy planning. The non-linear interaction between meteorological conditions has necessitated intelligent predictive models. However, existing studies focused on machine learning (ML) models in their black-box nature, with limited interpretability of the impact of climatic-drivers, climatic-demand interactions, and hidden consumption regimes. This research fills this gap through an integrated framework that combines seasonal hypothesis-testing, k-means clustering, Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based interpretability, and advanced predictive modeling using XGBoost, Random Forest (RF), long-short term memory (LSTM), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Autoregressive Integrated moving average (ARIMA). The seasonal hypothesis-testing using ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD revealed statistically significant differences in energy consumption across seasons, with peak-demand during winter and summer extremes. SHAP-based feature ranking identified temperature and humidity as the most influential drivers of electricity-demand. The k-means clustering revealed three distinct groups/clusters, which reflect the climatic-consumption scenarios. The ensemble learning (RF and XGBoost) exhibited the lowest training-error. RF had the best training performance with MSE, RMSE, and MAE values of 1.6484, 1.2839, and 0.8480. The data-driven insights in this study provide useful intelligence that supports critical decision-making through a proper understanding of the residential climatic-consumption dynamics. • ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD revealed a significant difference in consumption across seasons • k-means clustering reveals 3 distinct climatic-consumption patterns and regimes • SHAP revealed temperature as a dominant consumption driver • The random forest gave the best training performance with RMSE = 1.2839 • The framework facilitates climate-sensitive demand-side management and planning.

title: Spatial difference, dynamic evolution and influencing factors of carbon emission efficiency in China at the provincial level
abstract: As the world’s largest carbon emitter, China is actively pursuing its goals of carbon peaking and carbon neutrality. This has necessitated the analysis of the spatial and temporal differences in interprovincial carbon emission efficiency (CEE). This study develops a multimethod analytical framework to systematically investigate the static differences, dynamic evolution, and influencing factors of CEE across 30 provincial-level administrative regions in China from 2007 to 2021. Results demonstrate the national average CEE fluctuating between 0.878 and 1.093, with the central region exhibiting the highest mean efficiency at 0.9627 from a static perspective. Considerable disparities are observed between the eastern and western regions. Moreover, high-CEE regions are observed to suppress CEE growth in neighboring low-CEE areas. The Gini coefficient decomposition method reveals inter-regional differences as the main source of the overall inequality, accounting for 67.31% on average. Urbanization and industrial upgrading are observed to be the drivers of CEE, with population density being the strongest suppressor. GDP per capita and technological development are observed to contribute to regional CEE disparities via considerable negative spatial spillover effects. These findings provide a valuable basis for coordinating regional carbon emission reductions in China.

title: North Africa as an emerging green hydrogen hub: Algeria in focus
abstract: North Africa is emerging as a pivotal geoeconomic link in transcontinental energy flows across Europe, Asia, and Africa. This study evaluates the regional energy landscape, renewable resource endowment, and existing infrastructure in North Africa to identify key conditions enabling development of a green-hydrogen hub, with emphasis on Algeria as a core contributor to a trans-Mediterranean hydrogen corridor. The analysis shows that abundant solar and wind resources, proximity to European markets, and extensive natural gas pipeline and port systems create favorable conditions for cost-competitive green hydrogen production and large-scale export. The dense domestic gas network and existing trans-Mediterranean pipelines in Algeria provide practical pathways for hydrogen transport. However, the region faces persistent challenges, including slow renewable energy deployment, limited grid flexibility, and geopolitical uncertainty. The study concludes that realizing hydrogen potential in North Africa requires firm local industrial demand, coordinated regional governance, and long-term offtake agreements with shared infrastructure investments with the European Union. The findings support evidence-based development of the North Africa–Europe hydrogen corridor and design of regional energy strategies. • Abundant solar and wind resources support green hydrogen potential in North Africa. • The gas pipeline network in Algeria forms a backbone for a regional hydrogen hub. • Limited renewable expansion and pipeline repurposing remain key technical barriers. • Regional cooperation and EU collaboration are vital for hydrogen development.

title: Synergistic utilization of bauxite residue (red mud) and multiple solid wastes for low carbon precast concrete materials: Mechanical performance, mechanism and sustainability assessment
abstract: This study investigates the performance and mechanism of bauxite residue (red mud) and multiple solid wastes as active cement replacements in precast concrete. The effects of mixing ratio, water-to-binder ratio, and steam-curing temperature on mechanical properties and microstructural evolution were systematically evaluated. Results showed that incorporating 10–20% red mud significantly accelerates early hydration under 45–60 °C steam curing, enabling demoulding strength above 15 MPa within 8 h. Microstructural characterization reveals that the enhancement originates from the alkali–thermal synergistic mechanism: alkali released from red mud promote dissolution of fly ash glass phases and formation of C–(A)–S–H gels, which interweave with AFt to generate a dense microstructure. A suitable steam curing temperature will further enhance this synergistic effect. This synergistic hydration not only improves early mechanical performance but also supports stable long-term strength development. Sustainability assessment further indicated that the optimized mix design reduces carbon emissions by 46.1% and lowers material cost by 40.8% compared with the pure cement system. Overall, this study clarifies the alkali-thermal synergistic hydration mechanism in solid-waste-based precast concrete and demonstrates an effective pathway for large-scale synergistic utilization of industrial solid wastes such as red mud. • Reveals alkali–thermal synergistic hydration enabling efficient solid wastes utilization. • Synergistic effect accelerates hydration achieving 8 h demoulding strength exceeding 15 MPa. • Adding 10–20% red mud can balance early strength gain and long-term strength development. • Cuts carbon emissions by 46.1% and reduces material cost by 40.8% versus pure cement.

title: Energy, economic, and environmental evaluations on paper industry decarbonization by implementing electrolytic hydrogen
abstract: Paper mills are considered Hard-to-Abate sectors due to their high energy demand and reliance on fossil fuels, making cost-effective decarbonization challenging. This paper explores the potential of using hydrogen as a viable solution to reduce carbon dioxide emissions of a paper mill through a case study. A methodological approach is proposed to evaluate the technical, economic, and environmental performances of a hydrogen supply chain that includes an electrolysis unit powered by a photovoltaic plant. The hydrogen is blended with natural gas in a cogeneration plant, which supplies the electrical and thermal demands needed for the paper production process. Based on the technical analysis, the optimal sizes of the photovoltaic plant and the electrolysis unit were estimated at 45.6 MW and 16.1 MW, respectively, to achieve a hydrogen production of 1553 t/year. The environmental evaluation enabled the calculation of the avoided carbon dioxide emissions, which are equal to 9797 t/year. The economic assessment allowed to estimate the levelized cost of hydrogen, which is 4.24 €/kg. Finally, the break-even analysis highlighted the need for economic and financial instruments, including incentives for green hydrogen production and mechanisms aimed at supporting emissions reduction, to ensure that the industry grows in a sustainable, competitive, and resilient manner. • A novel integrated framework assessing hydrogen feasibility in a paper mill • 45.6 MW photovoltaic plant and 16 MW electrolyzer provide 1.5 kt/year of hydrogen • In the optimal configuration, the levelized cost of hydrogen is equal to 4.24 €/kg • Hydrogen in the paper mill enables an annual carbon dioxide reduction of 9.8 kt • A 0.6 €/kg hydrogen production incentive is required to ensure economic viability

title: Highly efficient continuous gas-phase dehydrogenation of formic acid by Ni induces β-Mo2C to α-MoC structural transformation
abstract: Formic acid (FA) is a promising hydrogen storage carrier for high power density hydrogen fuel cells. However, dehydrogenation of FA usually produces CO by-products that poison the catalyst. The prevention of FA decomposition into CO within high-temperature proton exchange membrane (HT-PEM) systems operating at 130–200°C remains a formidable scientific challenge. Here, we propose a Ni doping-induced active phase transition of molybdenum carbide on carbon-based catalysts, enhancing hydrogen production from FA. Ni-MoC/NC achieves complete FA conversion at 190 °C, maintaining stable catalytic performance over 170 hours. In MoC/NC, Mo primarily exists as β-Mo 2 C and γ-Mo 2 N, while in Ni-MoC/NC, it predominantly forms α-MoC and γ-Mo 2 N. XRD and XPS analyses reveal that Ni doping induces the transformation of β-Mo 2 C into α-MoC, improving catalytic performance. Mechanistic studies identify HCOO* as a key intermediate in FA dehydrogenation on Ni-MoC/NC. The catalyst promotes the dissociation of HCOOH* into HCOO*, reduces the energy barrier for HCOO* conversion to CO 2 *, and inhibits CO by-product formation, accelerating FA dehydrogenation. These findings highlight Ni-MoC/NC as a robust catalyst for efficient hydrogen production. • Ni-promoted Mo-soybean solid-phase reaction converts β-Mo 2 C to α-MoC. • Catalyst gives 100% FA conversion and H 2 selectivity; 170 h at 190 °C. • Reveals functional group evolution and intermediate formation in FA dehydrogenation.

title: Unraveling multi-channel oxygen species activation pathways on spinel catalysts: From surface redox dynamics to reactivity modulation in VOCs oxidation processes
abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) play a central role in redox catalysis over spinel oxides, contributing to both thermal and electrochemical oxidation processes, especially in the removal of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Species such as lattice oxygen (O latt ) and adsorbed oxygen (O ads ) govern catalytic performance through structure-dependent activation and regeneration pathways. This review critically evaluates three major strategies for tuning ROS behavior: surface defect engineering, lattice doping and interface construction. This study delves into the activation and migration mechanisms of diverse oxygen species at the surface and bulk phases of metal oxides from an electronic perspective. Using spinel oxides renowned for their complex and abundant surface-active oxygen species as research object, we systematically synthesized the molecular dynamics (MD) and density functional theory (DFT) calculations reported in existing literature to elucidate the intrinsic correlations between oxygen species and the reaction rates of the catalytic oxidation processes of various VOCs. Based on existing research, this work proposes rational design principles for spinel-based catalysts in oxidation reactions, aiming to advance the rational development of next-generation VOCs oxidation catalysts. • Reviewing strategies to regulate reactive oxygen species on spinel oxides. • Elucidating the dynamic synergy of oxygen species in VOCs mineralization. • Proposing a roadmap for robust catalyst design toward industrial applications.

title: CO2 assisted steam gasification for hydrogen-rich syngas from rice straw: Evolution of carbon structure and its effect
abstract: CO 2 -assisted steam gasification of rice straw (RS) offers a promising approach for both the sustainable utilization of rice straw and the reduction of CO 2 emissions. This study investigates the transformation of RS during pyrolysis and gasification in a fixed-bed reactor, with structural changes observed through solid-state 13 C nuclear magnetic resonance and Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy. The gas composition is analyzed by gas GC, and covalent bonds are quantified through carbon structure and elemental analysis. The results demonstrate that steam acts as a key reactant in the gasification process, significantly enhancing the pyrolysis of RS and leading to higher hydrogen yields. CO 2 serves as an oxidant above 500°C, oxygenating aromatic rings and initiating ring-opening reactions to form active C(O) intermediates that are crucial for hydrogen production. The hydrogen yield increases similarly to H 2 O gasification, while methane and carbon monoxide decrease significantly after gasification over 700°C. The H 2 /CO ratio improves from 0.64 in N 2 to 1.46 in H 2 O, and further to 1.71 in CO 2 -H 2 O at 700°C. CO 2 -assisted steam gasification optimizes the reactive interface activity, promoting the selective formation of hydrogen and improving the efficiency of the gasification process. Furthermore, CO 2 plays a pivotal role in enhancing the formation of active C(O) intermediates, which further facilitates the production of high-purity hydrogen. The process also induces the formation of a regular micro-pore structure, improving the overall efficiency and selectivity of directional hydrogen generation. • Steam is acted as the reactant and catalyst for gasification of RS. • CO 2 -assisted steam gasification significantly enhances hydrogen yield and purity. • CO 2 -assisted steam gasification optimizes reactive interface activity for gas reaction. • CO 2 improves the active C(O) intermediates for Hydrogen production.

title: Goethite-modified peanut shell biochar for selective phosphate recovery from digestate-derived permeate via membrane capacitive deionization
abstract: Selective phosphate recovery from digestate-derived effluents remains a technical bottleneck due to high background salinity and strong multi-anion competition. To address this, waste peanut shells were valorized into activated biochar and functionalized with goethite (α-FeOOH) to form a regenerable anode for membrane capacitive deionization (MCDI). When treating real anaerobic-digestion membrane-bioreactor (AD-MBR) permeate, the optimized 20 wt% α-FeOOH/BC anode achieved a phosphate enrichment factor of 11.46 ± 0.61 and selectivity factors ≥ 5.47 against major competing anions, producing a phosphate-rich concentrate of 695–790 mg L −1 . The process remained stable over 20 adsorption-desorption cycles, maintaining a desorption efficiency of 0.94 ± 0.03 and negligible Fe loss (0.59% of the initial Fe inventory). XPS analysis confirmed the mechanism involved reversible inner-sphere Fe–O–P complexation. The mean recovery-specific energy consumption was 9.07 ± 0.64 kWh kg −1 -P. Overall, this study establishes a sustainable waste-to-resource framework, demonstrating that α-FeOOH-functionalized biochar electrodes can effectively couple agricultural residue valorization with closed-loop phosphate recovery from complex digestate permeates. • Peanut-shell biochar supports goethite anode for phosphate-selective MCDI. • Phosphate selectivity (coefficient > 5.47) was achieved in real AD-MBR permeate. • Stable 20-cycle cycling achieved 94% desorption efficiency and 0.6% Fe loss. • XPS indicates reversible Fe–O–P binding with re-hydroxylation on regeneration • Competitive SEC (∼9.1 kWh kg -1 -P) supported sustainable nutrient looping.

title: Comparative life cycle assessment of Rankine-based Carnot batteries and lithium-ion batteries for grid-scale energy storage
abstract: Carnot batteries are investigated as a potential alternative to electro-chemical batteries for grid-scale electricity storage, which is a crucial element to the decarbonisation of energy systems via variable renewable energy sources. In this work, a comprehensive life cycle assessment of the construction and end-of-life phases of two Rankine-based Carnot battery system configurations is presented, comparing water and thermal oil as hot thermal energy storage fluid. Both are benchmarked against lithium-ion batteries as the most common electro-chemical battery alternative. To enhance the robustness of the analysis, uncertainties in the input parameters and life cycle inventory data are explicitly considered and analysed. The deterministic results show that the Carnot battery using water as hot storage fluid performs best in 13 of 18 environmental impact categories. For example, the climate change impact is up to 23 % lower. Thermal energy storage systems are identified as the dominant contributors, accounting for more than 50 % of the environmental impact across most impact categories. The stochastic results considering uncertainty show that the Carnot battery with water tends to have environmental impacts on par with lithium-ion batteries, while the Carnot battery with thermal oil tends to perform the worst. • Component-wise LCA of Carnot batteries with uncertainty consideration • Water-based Carnot batteries achieve lowest impact in 13 of 18 midpoint categories • Impacts considering uncertainties are less conclusive • Thermal oil-based Carnot batteries have the highest environmental impacts • Thermal energy storage contributes most to the environmental impact

title: Thermodynamic and economic assessment of a solar-assisted ORC-hydrogen system for natural gas pressure energy recovery
abstract: A significant amount of pressure energy is wasted during natural gas pressure reduction, while the cold energy generated from expansion is utilized inefficiently and typically relies on fossil fuel combustion for reheating. To address these challenges, this study proposes a pressure energy recovery system designated Int-ORC that combines an Organic Rankine Cycle, photovoltaic power generation, and alkaline water electrolysis for hydrogen production. Based on actual operational data from a pressure reduction station in Inner Mongolia, China, a coupled thermodynamic and economic model was developed using MATLAB to evaluate system performance. The Int-ORC system is compared against a basic pressure energy recovery system designated Ref. A and a pressure energy recovery system with hydrogen production designated Ref. B. The results show that the Int-ORC system achieves primary energy saving rates of 3.81 in summer and 2.98 in winter, representing improvements of 0.14 and 0.81 over Ref. A and Ref. B, respectively. The cold energy is fully utilized, achieving zero fossil fuel consumption. Hydrogen production rates reach 18.41 m 3 /h in summer and 18.78 m 3 /h in winter, both outperforming Ref. B. This study provides a technical foundation for the construction of next-generation gas stations integrating power generation, hydrogen production, and hydrogen blending functionalities.

title: Design of low carbon development path for urban power system based on system dynamics: A case study of Jinan City, China
abstract: The continuous advancement of urbanization is usually accompanied by a steady increase in urban energy consumption. A complex multi-factor influence network is embedded behind this positive correlation. By taking Jinan as the research object, a system dynamics model is constructed, which considers economy, energy, environment and other factors related to the urban power system (UPS). With electricity supply and demand as the clue, the key factors affecting carbon emissions of the UPS are traced. Low-carbon development path for the UPS is also designed. 4 key factors are identified, and they are categorized into 3 regulatory factors: industrial structure, energy storage technology, energy consumption intensity. They are used to design development scenario. In the suitable scenario combination, the GDP of the tertiary sector grows by 7% annually, energy storage equipment prices drop by 7% annually, the electricity consumption per GDP in the secondary sector drop by 3.3% annually. The average carbon emission intensity of the UPS can be reduced to 251.52 kgCO 2 /10 4 CNY during 2021-2025. The final suggestion for the UPS low-carbon development path is put forward: "industrial structure→energy consumption intensity→energy storage technology". These conclusions can provide scientific guidance for the low-carbon development of the UPS.

title: Eco-efficient valorization of gold tailings: A low-carbon binder with high early strength and reduced carbon footprint
abstract: To address the demand for low-carbon binders with high early-age strength for gold tailings cementation, a sulfur-aluminum-ferric gold tailings cementitious material (SGCM) was developed using low-carbon sulfur-aluminum-ferric cementitious material (LSCM), gypsum, lime, and ordinary Portland cement (OPC). The binder composition was optimized through ternary and quaternary system experiments, and the corresponding hydration mechanism was investigated by isothermal calorimetry, X-ray diffraction, thermogravimetric analysis and scanning electron microscopy. The optimal proportion was identified as an LSCM:(gypsum + lime):OPC mass ratio of 1:1.2:0.4. At a cement-to-sand ratio of 1:4 and a filling concentration of 71%, the optimized SGCM achieved compressive strengths of 3.40 MPa at 3 d and 8.26 MPa at 28 d, showing superior early-age strength and competitive long-term strength compared with representative cementitious systems reported in previous studies. In addition, when applied at a reduced cement-to-sand ratio of 1:6, SGCM maintained compressive strength comparable to that of the OPC system at 1:4, while reducing the carbon emission factor by 70.2%; under the self-produced LSCM scenario, the material cost was further reduced by 15.0%. Mechanistic analyses revealed that increasing gypsum and lime contents promoted AFt formation but also transformed AFt into shorter and thicker crystals, whereas OPC incorporation enhanced early hydration, increased C-S-H generation, and densified the microstructure. AFt provided skeletal support, while C-S-H provided filling and bonding, and their synergy governed the strength development of SGCM. • Developed a low-carbon high early-strength binder for gold tailings cementation. • Achieved superior 3 d (3.40 MPa) and 28 d (8.26 MPa) compressive strengths. • Reduced carbon emission factor by 70.2% and cost by 15.0% at comparable strength. • Revealed synergistic mechanism of AFt skeleton and C-S-H gel adhesion.

title: Synergistic hybrid systems of 2D-MOFs and TMDs for advanced energy harvesting
abstract: The globally trending move towards renewable energy sources requires materials capable of harvesting, storing, and converting energy in a competent fashion and yet scalable, robust, and affordable. Two-dimensional metal-organic frameworks (2D-MOFs) and transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have been promising materials for photovoltaics, thermoelectrics, piezoelectrics, and triboelectrics, respectively, but both material families are plagued by intrinsic drawbacks. MOFs have high area and chemical tailoring but are hampered by low conductivity, and TMDs have robust electronic and catalytic functionality but are plagued by stability and scalability issues. Recent developments indicate hybrid 2D-MOF/TMD systems are capable of offsetting failings by encapsulating complementary properties, facilitating superior charge separation, band alignment engineering, and enhancement in environmental tolerance. This review critically examines the structural, electronic, and functional synergies of 2D-MOF/TMD hybrids with emphasis on synthesis strategies, interface engineering, defect modulation, and emerging applications in diverse energy harvesting platforms. Comparative analyses of existing studies highlight how hybrid architectures deliver higher power densities, longer cycling stability, and superior device integration relative to their parent materials. Critical issues such as scalable synthesis, long-term stability under operating conditions, and reproducible device-level integration are also mentioned as hurdles in commercialization. Experimental design, computational modeling, and machine learning are envisaged in the future to accelerate discovery and optimization of high-performance hybrids. Bridging the gap between applied engineering and basic research, 2D-MOF/TMD hybrids are a paradigm shift in multifunctional materials and a promising avenue towards next-generation sustainable energy technology.

title: Development of similarity and normalization models for spray characteristics with the momentum equation as the theoretical basis
abstract: Fuel atomization in diesel engines can be significantly improved by elevating the injection pressure and decreasing the nozzle orifice diameter. Addressing the limited research on mathematical modeling within the regime of 300-MPa-level injection and micro-holes, this paper presents a comprehensive study on the similarity and normalization of spray evolution for ultra-high-pressure micro-nozzle configurations. In the experiments, key parameters such as injection pressure difference, ambient density, and hole diameter were selected as the main variables. The spray development process was divided into two main stages, and the similarity criteria and normalization equations for spray characteristics were derived accordingly. Combined with the DBI (Diffused Back-Illumination) method and processing technology, experimental data were obtained to verify the reliability of the established models. The experimental results show that both the similarity conversion results and normalization results of the derived mathematical models exhibit good consistency with the experimental data. This study can provide theoretical support for the optimization and spray characteristic prediction of ultra-high pressure small high-speed diesel engines.

title: Hydrogen-powered UAVs: A systematic review of technological advancements, safety frameworks, and future prospects
abstract: Hydrogen aviation stands out as a crucial avenue for achieving deep decarbonization; however, its commercial adoption is currently hindered by substantial logistical and economic challenges. In this context, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) emerge as a promising initial market for hydrogen propulsion, leveraging the technology's high gravimetric energy density and the comparatively lower barriers to certification that align well with UAV operational requirements. This study conducts a comprehensive review of the research and development landscape for hydrogen-powered UAVs, examining their application potential, key technological advancements, lifecycle carbon reduction capabilities, and safety considerations. The findings indicate that hydrogen-powered UAVs are particularly well-suited for applications in power line inspection, logistics and distribution, and agriculture, primarily owing to their extended endurance and ability to operate across a wide temperature range. Additionally, the zero-carbon operation of these UAVs underscores their significant carbon reduction potential from a lifecycle assessment viewpoint. Importantly, safety considerations for hydrogen-powered UAVs necessitate a systematic approach that addresses three critical dimensions: design requirements, hydrogen storage and refueling protocols, and adherence to regulations, codes, and standards (RCSs). While hydrogen-powered UAVs exhibit vast development potential and promise substantial reductions in carbon emissions, collaborative engagement among diverse stakeholders will be essential to propel technological innovation, enhance infrastructure development, and support favorable policy frameworks.

title: Sulfate resistance of circulating fluidized bed fly ash-based hybrid alkaline cement: Contrasting mechanisms in Na2SO4 and MgSO4 environments
abstract: Traditional cement production remains a significant contributor to CO 2 emissions, therefore, there is a need to explore new types of low-carbon cementitious materials. Hybrid alkaline cement (HAC), a novel cement-based binder with a low carbon footprint, is synthesized from less than 30 wt.% ordinary Portland cement (OPC) in combination with over 70 wt.% supplementary cementitious materials. HAC can achieve a shorter setting time and higher mechanical strength than OPC and geopolymer pastes and has been used in rapid construction and repair engineering. However, it remains crucial to determine its suitability for use in saline soil environments. In this study, the adaptability of circulating fluidized bed fly ash (CA)-based HAC (CHAC), OPC and CA-based geopolymer (CG) in the sulfate environment was compared. The temporal and spatial evolution laws of CHAC microstructures in different concentrations of sodium sulfate and magnesium sulfate solutions were elucidated. Results show that the mechanical strength of CHAC can continue to develop even after being immersed in sodium sulfate solution for 120 d, which was 1.39 and 2.62 times greater than that of OPC and CG, respectively. This is because the conversion of C-A-S-H gel into N-A-S-H gel and the crystallization of gypsum optimized the pore structure and densified the matrix of the hardened CHAC. In contrast, MgSO 4 exposure produced a distinctly magnesium-driven deterioration process. Mg 2+ promoted brucite precipitation and the degradation of C-A-S-H gels, generating expansive stress and increasing the total porosity of the CHAC matrix. These coupled effects weakened the matrix and reduced the resistance of CHAC to MgSO 4 attack. Nevertheless, CHAC still exhibited higher resistance to magnesium sulfate attack than OPC and CG. These findings confirm that CHAC demonstrates better sulfate resistance compared to OPC and CG, highlighting its potential as a sustainable and durable alternative to traditional cementitious materials.

title: Impact of metal-based hydrogen production on the hydrogen energy industry chain
abstract: Metal-steam thermochemical hydrogen production technology (referred to as metal-based hydrogen production) utilizes the reaction between metals and steam to efficiently produce green hydrogen, offering advantages such as convenient hydrogen production, mild production conditions, abundant metal raw materials, low transportation costs, and high safety. This paper systematically analyzes the disruptive impact of this technology on the four segments of the hydrogen energy industry chain—"production-storage-transportation-utilization"—and explores its advantages in terms of cost, safety, and reliability. Research indicates that metal-based hydrogen production technology is expected to reshape the structure of the hydrogen energy industry chain, significantly reduce the cost of hydrogen use, and provide key technical support for the large-scale application of hydrogen energy and the achievement of carbon neutrality goals. It is projected that by 2030, the cost of metal-based hydrogen production will drop below $2.19/kg, making it competitive with renewable energy electrolysis for water splitting.

title: Nanofluids as next-generation geothermal working fluids: Benchmarking against water-based systems, phase change materials (PCMs), and supercritical CO2 (SC-CO2)
abstract: Geothermal energy is a promising clean energy source because of its ample reserves and minimal carbon footprint. However, its effective extraction relies on the stimulated reservoir's size and the thermophysical properties of the working fluid. Mainly water and, in some cases, SC-CO 2 are used as a working fluid, but PCMs and nanofluids could be an alternative. Most existing reviews treat these candidate fluids separately, making it difficult to compare options using consistent criteria that account for thermal performance, hydraulic penalties, operational risks, and deployment feasibility. Therefore, this review evaluates thermophysical properties of geothermal fluids, including water/brine, SC-CO 2 , PCMs, and nanofluids, across various reservoir and wellbore configurations, using a framework that clarifies tradeoffs and readiness barriers to help identify the most suitable fluid for each geothermal application. Water/brines have high specific heat and conductivity but face corrosion and scaling problems. SC-CO 2 ,’s low viscosity and high expansivity boost heat extraction by about 50% in moderate-temperature reservoirs, but its low thermal conductivity can limit heat uptake and reduce delivered temperature in practice. PCMs store latent heat for thermal management, yet phase segregation and cycling degradation limit their use in geothermal systems. Nanofluids can boost thermal conductivity by up to 40%, improving heat transfer, but face high viscosity and pumping power costs. Nevertheless, with suitable nanoparticle type and concentration, nanofluids can greatly improve heat extraction, showing promise as next-generation geothermal fluids. Accordingly, this review discusses feasible solutions to key challenges of nanofluids and identifies research gaps and future directions to support their ongoing development.

title: Improving the efficiency of CO2 utilization in vertical farming via CFD modelling with consideration of leaf microstructure
abstract: : Vertical farming (VF), as a promising solution to mitigating the multifaceted challenges posed by global population growth and urbanization, needs supplementing carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), an essential substrate for photosynthesis, to promote plant growth. Optimizing the CO 2 supply to reduce operational costs relies on accurate modelling of CO 2 distribution and intake within VF chambers. For such an objective, this research constructed an innovative computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model that can explicitly incorporate the effects of leaf microstructure on CO 2 absorption to simulate CO 2 interactions between plants and environment more accurately. After validation, the model was employed to investigate CO 2 distribution, photosynthetic rate, and total CO 2 consumption, using wheat as a studied crop due to data availability. Compared to previous models that ignored CO 2 diffusion within leaves, the new model shows a decrease in the daily CO 2 uptake by 8.1%, and consequently the consumption of pure CO 2 is reduced by 8.5%. Such findings reveal that incorporating the leaf microstructure is important to improve the accuracy in modelling CO 2 supplementation and avoid the overestimation of CO 2 utilization efficiency.

title: Study on the Influence of Paraffin-Based Composite Walls on Thermal Performance in Solar Greenhouses
abstract: This study developed a paraffin phase-change material (PCM) composite wall for solar greenhouses by incorporating paraffin into the back wall interlayer. Using finite element simulations and comparative experiments with different wall structures (The conventional wall system comprises sintered bricks, extruded polystyrene (XPS) boards, and cement mortar finishing layers), we analyzed the thermal performance of this design (The tests were conducted from May to June 2024 and from November to December 2024 in Daqing, Heilongjiang Province, China). Numerical calculations showed the paraffin composite wall achieved a total thermal resistance of 2.49 (m 2 ·K)/W, representing a 4.8% improvement over conventional walls. Simulation results indicated 0.24-1.09°C higher average daily temperatures in PCM-equipped greenhouses. Experimental data confirmed a 0.61°C increase in average daily temperature under sunny conditions compared to traditional designs. In the economic benefit assessment, the labor cost for the paraffin composite wall solar greenhouse throughout the entire heating season is approximately 2.5 yuan per square meter. The strong agreement among theoretical, simulated, and experimental results validates the thermal enhancement effect of paraffin composite walls. These findings demonstrate the potential of PCM-integrated walls for improving greenhouse thermal performance and provide a theoretical basis for applying phase-change materials in agricultural structures.

title: Mechanistic insights into catalytic co-pyrolysis of cellulose and polyethylene via ReaxFF molecular dynamics simulations
abstract: The catalytic co-pyrolysis of biomass and plastics is a promising strategy for improving waste conversion and regulating product distribution. In this study, ReaxFF molecular dynamics simulations were used to compare cellulose-polyethylene co-pyrolysis systems with and without Fe 2 O 3 nanocluster, aiming to obtain atomistic insights into the role of Fe 2 O 3 under accelerated high-temperature simulation conditions. Product analysis showed that in Fe 2 O 3 catalytic co-pyrolysis system, the tendency toward the formation of light liquid products became more pronounced within the temperature range of 2200-2600 K, which was associated with the competition between rapid cracking and secondary fragment-growth or recombination processes. Bond-evolution analysis indicated that Fe 2 O 3 facilitated the overall decay of C-C and C-H bonds. The apparent activation energies derived from the C-C and C-H bond-count decay model decreased from 100.69 to 86.86 kJ/mol in the non-catalytic system to 88.72 and 77.87 kJ/mol in the catalytic system, respectively. Fe-O bond tracking further suggested temperature-dependent lattice-oxygen loss, oxygen exchange with cellulose-derived oxygen, and the formation of oxygen-deficient Fe sites, which contributed to the enhanced formation of H 2 O and CO. Reaction pathway analysis suggested that Fe 2 O 3 modified the formation routes of CH 4 , C 2 H 4 , C 2 H 2 , and CH 2 O by promoting oxygen transfer and altering the evolution of oxygen-containing intermediates. These results provide simulation-based mechanistic insights into Fe 2 O 3 catalyze cellulose-polyethylene co-pyrolysis and offer hypotheses for future experimental validation.

title: Carbon-based electrode materials for sustainable capacitive deionization: Energy efficiency, performance metrics, and scalability challenges
abstract: Growing freshwater scarcity, rapid industrialization, population growth, and climate change have intensified the demand for sustainable and energy-efficient desalination technologies. Among emerging electrochemical water-treatment approaches, capacitive deionization (CDI) and flow-electrode capacitive deionization (FCDI) have attracted significant attention because of their low operating voltage, modular design, operational flexibility, and potential for resource recovery. Despite substantial progress, a comprehensive understanding of how electrode materials, charge-storage mechanisms, system configurations, and operational parameters collectively influence desalination performance and scalability remains fragmented across the literature. This review critically examines the development of CDI and FCDI technologies, with particular emphasis on carbon-based electrode materials and their role in electrochemical desalination. The fundamental mechanisms governing ion removal, including electric double-layer formation, co-ion effects, and Faradaic charge storage, are discussed alongside the evolution of major CDI architectures, such as membrane CDI, inverted CDI, hybrid CDI, desalination batteries, and FCDI. Recent advances in carbon-based electrodes, flow-electrode materials, membrane integration, reactor design, and process optimization are systematically evaluated in relation to desalination efficiency, ion selectivity, energy consumption, and operational stability. Emerging applications in wastewater treatment, selective ion separation, nutrient recovery, and resource recovery are also highlighted. Current challenges associated with electrode degradation, membrane fouling, flow-electrode conductivity, process standardization, scale-up, and commercialization are critically discussed. Finally, future research directions involving advanced material design, intelligent process optimization, renewable-energy integration, and hybrid treatment systems are identified to support the practical deployment of CDI and FCDI technologies for sustainable water treatment and resource management.

title: Rock mechanics–driven interpretable machine learning framework for preliminary seal integrity screening in geological CO2 storage
abstract: Caprock integrity assessment is essential for ensuring the long-term security of geological CO 2 storage; however, early-stage evaluation is often challenged by limited and heterogeneous subsurface datasets. This study proposes an interpretable machine learning framework for preliminary caprock integrity screening using limited rock mechanics data from the 31/5–7 Eos well-core of the Northern Lights CO 2 storage project. An unsupervised learning workflow was first employed to reconstruct Safe, Transitional, and Risk integrity regimes through cluster validation and ambiguity-based boundary analysis. Multiple supervised learning algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and XGBoost, were subsequently developed and evaluated under stratified train/test split, Leave-One-Out Cross Validation (LOOCV), and repeated stratified cross-validation strategies. Random Forest demonstrated the most stable predictive behaviour across validation schemes, achieving balanced accuracies exceeding 0.86. Explainability analyses using Random Forest feature importance and SHAP consistently identified porosity and axial stress as dominant screening controls, suggesting coupled stress–structure interactions govern integrity behaviour within the studied dataset. Based on these observations, a Stress–Porosity Screening Score (SPSS) was developed as a simplified post hoc screening descriptor for rapid integrity evaluation. Statistical analyses demonstrated significant differentiation of SPSS across reconstructed integrity regimes ( p < 0.001). Decision-tree interpretation further enabled extraction of preliminary data-emergent screening pathways and threshold behaviour. Conclusively, the proposed methodology provides an interpretable and data-adaptive screening approach intended to support early-stage caprock assessment and guide subsequent detailed geomechanical investigations.

title: Battery thermal management of electric vehicles: A review and bibliometric analysis of liquid cooling methods
abstract: Thermal management plays a vital role in the operation of electric vehicle (EV) batteries, directly influencing their efficiency, safety, and market adoption. In real-world EV operation, inadequate thermal regulation can accelerate battery degradation and increase safety risks, highlighting the importance of effective battery thermal management system (BTMS) design. In response, extensive research explored liquid BTMSs for EV applications. Despite this growing body of research, a comprehensive overview that combines a critical review and a bibliometric analysis of EV liquid BTMS research remains scarce. This paper aims to address this gap by presenting a combined critical review and bibliometric investigation of recent trends and developments in EV liquid BTMSs. The review examines key aspects of liquid BTMSs, including system configurations, coolant types, performance enhancement methods, and hybrid configurations. The bibliometric analysis covers research and review publications included in the Scopus database from 2015 to 2025, extracted on the 29 th of October 2025. The technical review was updated separately to include selected 2026 publications. After screening, 472 publications strongly related to liquid BTMSs were identified. The analysis demonstrates continuous growth in the field with an annual growth rate of 40.97% and a low average document age of 3.19 years. China leads the research with 214 publications. Liquid BTMS keyword analysis highlights three main research themes: temperature control and coolant systems, EV applications and battery technologies, and battery modeling and simulation. Key research gaps include coupled electrothermal modeling and artificial intelligence-based predictive control. This review highlights recent advancements and research gaps that can guide future development of liquid BTMS design and optimization to improve EV performance and safety.

title: Pathways for Integrated Blue Hydrogen Production with CO2 Utilization: A Review
abstract: Hydrogen is considered a promising energy carrier for decarbonizing sectors that are difficult to electrify. Among the available production routes, steam reforming combined with CO 2 capture, commonly referred to as blue hydrogen, remains a practical near- to mid-term option, supported by its technological readiness, scalability, and compatibility with existing infrastructure. Despite these advantages, conventional configurations such as SR-CCS and SR-CCU are associated with considerable energy demands and increased process complexity, particularly in CO 2 regeneration, separation, and downstream handling. Recent progress has therefore focused on more effective integration of CO 2 capture and utilization within steam reforming systems. In this context, this review evaluates developments across different levels of process integration, including conventional SR-CCU, integrated configurations such as SR-ICCU, and intensified reactor concepts incorporating both ex situ and in situ CO 2 utilization. Particular attention is given to multifunctional reactor systems, including sorption-enhanced reforming, chemical looping reforming, and membrane-assisted processes, with emphasis on their roles in shifting reaction equilibrium, improving hydrogen purity, enhancing carbon utilization, and optimizing overall energy efficiency. Key challenges and future opportunities are discussed to support the development of efficient and low-carbon hydrogen production systems.

title: Non-Thermal Plasmas Activated Lattice Oxygen for Methane Partial Oxidation
abstract: Ceria (CeO 2 ) is a classic oxygen storage catalyst widely used in energy, environmental and chemical fields. However, the activation of ceria typically requires elevated temperatures, largely due to the slow kinetics of lattice oxygen migration from the bulk to the surface at low temperatures. Non-Thermal Plasmas (NTPs) offer a viable strategy to mitigate the thermodynamic and kinetic limitations associated with traditional thermal catalysis. Herein, we investigated the impact of the plasma field on reaction kinetics and lattice oxygen evolution of ceria in a methane partial oxidation process with a dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma catalytic system. The results indicate that the NTPs exhibit a "Dual-Path Effect" via simultaneously facilitating C-H bond dissociation of methane (reducing activation energy by 52.1% to 35.69 kJ·mol -1 ) and activating lattice oxygen via creating abundant oxygen vacancies in ceria. The NTPs lower the onset temperature of lattice oxygen release by 75°C and triples the bulk-to-surface migration rate of lattice oxygen. Consequently, methane conversion at 750°C is enhanced 6-fold compared to the thermal catalysis alone. This work provides an insight into developing thermochemical processes under mild conditions via NTPs intensification.

title: Extending catalyst lifetime through coke mitigation and magnesium-assisted regeneration in low-density polyethylene/biomass co-pyrolysis
abstract: Stable catalytic processes are needed to convert waste plastics and biomass into value-added fuels and chemicals, but coke-induced deactivation remains a major limitation for metal-acid zeolite catalysts. In this study, FeNi@HZ50 was modified by introducing Cu or Ca as a second metal to regulate coke evolution, forming 3Cu-FeNi@HZ50 and 3Ca-FeNi@HZ50. Compared with 3Cu-FeNi@HZ50, 3Ca-FeNi@HZ50 exhibited higher selectivity toward monocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (MAHs), lower polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon formation, and a weaker hard coke contribution, as revealed by temperature-programmed oxidation. The relative contents of MAHs and benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes (BTEX) in the liquid products over 3Ca-FeNi@HZ50 reached 58.98% and 45.19%, respectively. Moderate Ca loading promoted aromatization and suppressed deep condensation, whereas excessive Ca partially covered metal or acid sites and increased the retention of oxygenates and aliphatics. Under continuous feeding conditions, 3Ca-FeNi@HZ50 showed slower BTEX decay, less accumulation of heavy components, and weaker coke formation than FeNi@HZ50. To facilitate reuse, a magnesium-assisted regeneration process was developed by impregnating the deactivated catalyst with Mg before reactivation. This treatment improved micropore accessibility, shifted deposits toward more easily removable species, and enhanced cyclic stability. These findings establish an engineering-oriented strategy for extending the lifetime of metal-acid zeolite catalysts by coupling coke mitigation with regeneration reinforcement in catalytic co-pyrolysis.

title: Breaking the Recycling Bottleneck of Wind Turbine Blade Composites from a Full-Life-Cycle Closed-Loop Perspectives
abstract: The rapid expansion of global wind power installed capacity has resulted in enormous waste of wind turbine blades (WTBs) made of thermosetting resin matrix composites. Most existing review articles merely summarize recycling processes from a single dimension, lacking a full-chain systematic analysis that integrates intrinsic material mechanisms, techno-economic performance and top-level policy coordination. Taking full-life-cycle closed-loop resource valorization as the core research objective, this paper focuses on three pivotal scientific problems: (1) revealing the essential restrictive factors for blade recycling through microstructure characterization of raw materials; (2) establishing a multi-dimensional evaluation framework for four principal end-of-life (EOL) strategies, including direct reuse, mechanical recycling, pyrolysis, and chemical recycling, to systematically compare their advantages, limitations, and applicable scenarios; (3) clarifying the coupling relationship between the upfront design of recyclable resins/fibers and EOL recycling technologies, and proposing targeted countermeasures to fix defects in relevant industrial policies. This paper reviews existing blade recycling technologies from process principle, fiber damage and component property, and compares recycling routes for glass/carbon fiber composites. Based on advanced recyclable materials including dynamic covalent resins, thermoplastic matrices and bio-based reinforcements, it discusses the approach of source recyclable design to replace EOL waste treatment, and analyzes policy deficiencies concerning the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) system and regional industrial support.

title: Research on the carbon sequestration potential and performance of modified biochar promoting carbon capture artificial aggregates
abstract: Currently, due to the dense nature of the concrete matrix and the formation of a dense calcium carbonate layer during carbonation that hinders further CO 2 diffusion, the carbonation process of concrete takes a long time. Biochar (BC), characterized by its porous structure and chemical stability, has shown potential in improving the mechanical properties and carbon sequestration capacity of materials. However, the influence mechanism of BC obtained by different modification methods on material performance remains unclear. To address this, this study developed concrete waste-biochar aggregate (CWBA) using construction waste powder (CWP) and BC, and investigated the effect of different BC modification processes on the performance of CWBA. In this study, a BC dosage of 5% was adopted, and BC was treated by water washing and alkali modification, respectively, while an unmodified group was used as a control. The physical properties, single particle compressive strength, and CO 2 uptake of the prepared CWBA were evaluated through macro-experiments, and the mechanism was analyzed based on micro-experiments. Among all the tested groups, AM-C (alkali-modified BC, carbonation curing) and NB-C (non-biochar, carbonation curing) exhibited the highest aggregate densities. At 3 days, the WW (water-washed BC) group exhibited the greatest carbonation gain, while at 28 days, the AM group showed the greatest carbonation gain and the NB group the smallest; the strength could be increased by up to 851% after carbonation. These results demonstrate that BC modified by alkali treatment may destroy the biomass tar layer on its surface and release the pore structure, thereby better offsetting the reduction in CO 2 uptake caused by matrix densification during curing, and providing greater carbonation gain under long-term service conditions.

title: Research Progress in Novel Non-Haber-Bosch Ammonia Synthesis Technologies
abstract: Ammonia is indispensable to fertiliser production and is increasingly considered a hydrogen carrier and carbon-free fuel at the point of use. Yet, its conventional manufacture consumes high energy and emits high CO2. This review critically compares four emerging non-Haber-Bosch pathways: electrocatalysis, plasma catalysis, photocatalysis, and chemical looping ammonia synthesis. The performance of these pathways is evaluated using common criteria, including nitrogen activation, selectivity, productivity, energy efficiency, stability, feedstock requirements, and scalability. Electrocatalysis is constrained by nitrogen activation and the competing hydrogen evolution reaction; photocatalysis by limited light utilisation and charge recombination; plasma catalysis by product selectivity and electrical efficiency; and chemical looping by nitrogen-carrier kinetics, phase stability, and reactor integration. Particular attention is given to two-step plasma–electrochemical systems that decouple air activation to NO x from selective NO x reduction to NH 3 . Recent demonstrations at ampere-level current density and in scaled electrolyser stacks establish meaningful progress, but they do not yet prove system-level superiority over green-hydrogen Haber-Bosch synthesis. The practical value of this coupling route remains conditional on plasma energy efficiency, NO x capture and transfer, electrolyser durability, renewable-electricity supply, and full-chain techno-economic and life-cycle performance. The review therefore identifies comparable reporting metrics, evidence gaps, and research priorities for evaluating where each route may contribute to future centralised or distributed ammonia production.

title: Solar-Powered Integrated Mechanical and Thermal Vapor Compression Desalination for Water Production Enhancement: A Technical and Economic Evaluation
abstract: This study investigates a novel solar-driven hybrid desalination system integrating Mechanical Vapor Compression (MVC) and Thermal Vapor Compression (TVC) cycles. The configuration uses Photovoltaic/Thermal (PV/T) collectors to provide both electrical power to the MVC and thermal energy to the TVC, supplemented by a Parabolic Trough Collector (PTC). A mechanistic framework was developed, modeled, simulated, and validated in MATLAB to analyze the coupled thermo-electro-hydrodynamic behavior, a detailed thermodynamic and performance analysis, and techno-economic analysis under dynamic, environmental, and operational conditions. Key findings reveal that the integrated system achieves a peak freshwater production of at a solar irradiance of . The Performance Ratio ( ) reached a maximum of while the was optimized to a minimum of . Parametric analysis confirms that solar irradiance ( ) and mass flow rate are the most critical drivers of productivity. Utilizing the thermal energy recovered from the water-cooled PV/T system increased the desalination rate by 6.5% and enhanced the electrical and thermal energy supplied to the MVC and TVC systems by up to 20.4% and 11.3%, respectively. It also reduced the levelized cost of water by 6.1%. These improvements provide a sustainable pathway for increasing water production, improving cost competitiveness, and reducing environmental impacts.

title: In situ mechanochemical activation of alkaline solid wastes boosts CO2 mineralization and carbon sequestration
abstract: ABSTRACT Alkaline solid wastes (ASWs) have substantial potential for CO 2 mineralization, but their carbonation is often limited by sluggish kinetics, surface passivation, and poor utilization of reactive phases. Here, we developed an in situ mechanochemical activation-wet carbonation (MC) strategy to enhance CO 2 sequestration in representative ASWs, including steel slag (SS), red mud (RM), construction and demolition waste (CDW), and coal fly ash (CFA). MC continuously disrupted passivating carbonation layers, refined particles, and renewed reactive surfaces, thereby accelerating carbonation kinetics by 1-2 orders of magnitude and increasing carbonation potential utilization from <15% under conventional carbonation to 28-80%. The maximum CO 2 uptake increased from 7.7, 49, 21, and 2.2 g/kg to 97, 72, 55, and 25 g/kg for SS, RM, CDW, and CFA, respectively, with SS and CFA showing >11-fold enhancement. MC generally improved the immobilization of carbonate-forming metals such as Pb and Ba, although certain amphoteric or trace metals showed increased mobility due to mineral disruption and pH-driven dissolution. Nevertheless, all heavy metals (Ba, Cr, As, Pb, Cu, Zn, Cd, Se, Ni) remained at relatively low leaching levels. When scaled by annual ASW generation, MC showed a maximum global mitigation potential of approximately 225 Mt CO 2 /yr, 2.3 times that of conventional carbonation.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Network Framework for Performance Prediction and Parameter Identification of Microbial Fuel Cells
abstract: Bioelectrochemical systems (BES) such as microbial fuel cells (MFCs) offer a promising route for sustainable wastewater treatment and bioelectricity generation. However, MFC modeling faces a structural dichotomy: mechanistic models provide physical interpretability but suffer from difficult calibration, while data-driven approaches offer predictive flexibility at the cost of mechanistic transparency and limited extrapolation. To reconcile these paradigms, we developed BioElec-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that couples sparse experimental data with a differential-algebraic bioelectrochemical model that distinguishes bulk and biofilm substrate compartments through a mass-transfer coefficient. This paper presents the BioElec-PINN architecture and evaluates its performance on fed-batch MFCs treating synthetic winery wastewater across varying organic loads. We trained the network to jointly reconstruct model-conditioned latent states and estimate ten regularized cycle-specific kinetic, transport, and electrochemical parameters. The BioElec-PINN achieved calibration voltage normalized root mean square error NRMSE values of 0.048–0.100. The inferred parameter sets were subsequently transferred without recalibration to a Radau IIA solver (classical solver), whose forward trajectories showed close cycle-level agreement and supported the cross-formulation dynamic consistency of the learned mechanistic parameterization. A matched Direct multilayer perceptron MLP was additionally evaluated using an interleaved held-out protocol in which approximately 40% of the observations were retained for training and the remaining 60% were used exclusively for raw-data evaluation. The Direct MLP achieved lower pointwise interpolation errors, with mean voltage and chemical oxygen demand (COD) NRMSE values of 0.064 and 0.146, compared with 0.121 and 0.206 for the BioElec-PINN, respectively. A conditional residual-bootstrap analysis based on 20 complete BioElec-PINN retrainings was used to quantify parameter uncertainty. Thirty-three of the forty cycle-specific estimates exhibited relative 95% interval widths below 1%, while the bootstrap correlation structure revealed coordinated kinetic, mediator, and electrochemical parameter groups. However, the unconstrained MLP introduced non-monotonic COD trajectories in three cycles and physically inadmissible continuation outside the observed interval, including negative voltage and substantial COD rebound. In contrast, the BioElec-PINN preserved monotonic substrate depletion and coupled voltage–substrate dynamics while reconstructing model-conditioned latent states and estimating regularized cycle-specific effective parameters. The framework therefore provides a physically structured inverse-calibration component for future MFC digital twins, with raw-data performance, physical admissibility, parameter transferability, and conditional uncertainty evaluated explicitly.

title: Investigation of copper recovery from PCB pyrolysis char and waste cable wires to fabricate Pd-Cu membranes for hydrogen separation
abstract: Electronic waste represents an important secondary source of valuable metals; however, recovered copper is still predominantly directed toward conventional recycling rather than high-value functional applications. This study proposes an integrated circular strategy to convert PCB-derived Cu into functional Pd–Cu membranes through sequential pyrolysis, electrochemical recovery, and membrane fabrication for hydrogen separation. Pyrolysis at 500 °C produced 68.2 wt.% char and increased the Cu concentration from 4.9 to 9.2 wt.%. Subsequent electrolysis recovered high-purity Cu (99.3–99.6 wt.%), with a maximum recovery efficiency of 77.1% at 40 mA/cm 2 . The Cu recovery process generated 21.57 kg CO 2 -eq/kg Cu with pyrolysis and electrolysis contributing 56.4% and 43.6%, respectively, identifying pyrolysis as the primary opportunity for carbon reduction. The recovered Cu was successfully reused to fabricate Pd-Cu membranes, demonstrating its suitability for functional material applications. The Pd-Cu/NiF membrane achieved a maximum H 2 permeability of 2.74 × 10 -9 mol m -1 s -1 Pa -0.5 at 400 °C while the Cu-coated Pd-Cu membrane maintained a permeability of 2.09–2.35 × 10 -9 mol m -1 s -1 Pa -0.5 over 400–500 °C. During long-term operation, the Cu-coated Pd-Cu membrane stabilized after approximately 8 h, whereas the Pd-Cu/NiF membrane exhibited a progressive decrease in permeability. Overall, this work demonstrates the feasibility of converting electronic waste-derived Cu into functional Pd-Cu membranes, integrating metal recovery, carbon-footprint assessment, material reuse, and hydrogen separation within a circular pathway.
